Two hinges in series: a heart-rate hinge feeds a second hinge that adds systolic pressure (with a very small diabetes term), and the result enters the output score with weight -1.85 (direct edge from this part to the output).

Self-probe (typical case, real units): at sbp 120 mmHg the part is off at heart rates 60, 70 and 80 beats/min (values 0.00, 0.00, 0.00) and on from 90 beats/min (value 1.99, rising to 7.23 at 110); at sbp 160 mmHg it is already on at 60 beats/min (value 1.42), so high pressure alone turns it on.
In the whole model this is what makes a fast heart rate protective when pressure is high: at sbp 160 mmHg, raising heart rate from 60 to 110 beats/min lowers the predicted risk from 73% to below 1%.
The training data agree in that corner: the 38 training patients matching heart_rate > 90 and sbp > 145 have an outcome rate of 2.6% and a mean predicted risk of 1.2%.
The part acts on 921 of the 1500 training patients, and for them it changes the score by -3.49 on average (through this part).
